models.name: EXD-Knee v1.2 (Explicit Dynamics Articular Contact Model)
models.what_it_computes: Transient contact mechanics during gait and non-gait maneuvers using explicit time integration; outputs include contact pressure/area, shear traction, cross-shear index, subsurface stress in UHMWPE, and instantaneous post–cam impact loads.

models.name: EXD-WearGrow v2.0 (Adaptive Wear–Creep Growth Model)
models.what_it_computes: Cycle-by-cycle cumulative wear depth with surface evolution using explicit dynamics with adaptive remeshing; outputs include volumetric wear, directional wear maps, creep-induced deformation, and edge-loading progression under malalignment.

mechanisms.name: Articular surface wear during level walking (ISO-style input profiles)
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Determines long-term UHMWPE volume loss and surface topography that drive revision risk.

mechanisms.name: Peak contact stress in deep flexion under axial–rotational load
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Controls risk of subsurface yielding and accelerated fatigue wear during kneeling or high-flexion activities.

mechanisms.name: Edge-loading under varus malalignment with internal tibial rotation
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Concentrates load at the insert rim, elevating delamination and wear at the periphery.

mechanisms.name: Post–cam impact and sliding during stair descent and sit-to-stand
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Sets post stress and cam wear drivers that affect stability and debris generation in posterior-stabilized designs.

deviation.detail: Credibility scores are reported on a 0–12 scale with anchors at 3 (initially acceptable), 6 (adequate for comparative assessment), 9 (strong), and 12 (compelling).

expected_decision.outcome_source: We conclude that both models are strong to compelling for levelwalking and post–cam questions, and adequate to strong for highflexion and edgeloading questions, provided users remain within stated testcondition envelopes and acknowledge wider uncertainty for rimcontact predictions.

acceptance_criteria: deviation from laboratory metrics ≤10% with two or more independent datasets typically supports a 9–12

findings.mechanism: Articular surface wear during level walking (ISO-style input profiles)
spans: Energy balance checks tracked kinetic, internal, hourglass, contact, and artificial energies; cumulative artificial energy remained below 0.5% of the sum of kinetic and internal energies during level walking, 0.9% during deep flexion, 1.1% during rim loading, and 0.8% during post–cam impacts.

findings.mechanism: Articular surface wear during level walking (ISO-style input profiles)
spans: EXDWearGrow v2.0 extends the explicit dynamics kernel with a cyclebycycle update of the free surface via an Archardtype wear rule generalized for crossshear and counterface hardness, and a creep update driven by mean stress using a Findleytype law; adaptive remeshing maintains element quality as the surface evolves.

findings.mechanism: Articular surface wear during level walking (ISO-style input profiles)
spans: The wear–creep growth loop in EXDWearGrow v2.0 was exercised on canonical problems with known solutions: for a flatonflat crawler under uniform pressure, the accumulated wear depth over 1 Mc matched the Archard solution to within 1.9%; a wedge indentation creep test reproduced the Findley prediction to within 3.5% after 10,000 s equivalent time.

findings.mechanism: Articular surface wear during level walking (ISO-style input profiles)
spans: For level walking, refining the articular inplane mesh from 0.5 to 0.35 mm and halving the time step changed EXDKnee v1.2 midstance peak pressure by 1.6% and contact area by 2.3%; EXDWearGrow v2.0’s 5 Mc wear volume changed by 3.8%.

findings.mechanism: Peak contact stress in deep flexion under axial–rotational load
spans: For peak contact stress in deep flexion, a quasistaticplustran-sient protocol was used: flexion of 120°, axial load stepped to 2,800 N over 25 ms, followed by a 15 ms ramp of an internal tibial rotation to 15° with a superimposed 18 N·m torque, maintaining small AP shear (<60 N).

findings.mechanism: Edge-loading under varus malalignment with internal tibial rotation
spans: Rim loading was more sensitive: increasing penalty stiffness by 50% increased peak rim pressure by 4.5%, and shifting internal rotation from 5° to 6° increased rimcontact width by 7.9%.

findings.mechanism: Edge-loading under varus malalignment with internal tibial rotation
spans: For rim loading, the 95% interval for peak rim pressure widened to ±22% (EXDKnee v1.2), and the volumetric wear fraction at the rim varied with ±19% halfwidth (EXDWearGrow v2.0), reflecting strong amplification of small alignment and friction changes.

findings.mechanism: Post–cam impact and sliding during stair descent and sit-to-stand
spans: For post–cam impacts during stair descent, EXDKnee v1.2 reproduced instrumented cam peak forces of 950 ± 110 N with predicted 880–1,010 N across timing variations (7.4% median deviation).

findings.mechanism: Post–cam impact and sliding during stair descent and sit-to-stand
spans: For stairdescent cam impacts, transient kinetictointernal energy ratios peaked at 4.7% at engagement and settled to <2% within 4 ms.

findings.mechanism: Post–cam impact and sliding during stair descent and sit-to-stand
spans: Post–cam loads were measured via a custom instrumented cam with a uniaxial highbandwidth force transducer (10 kHz sampling), in series with highspeed video (2,000 fps) to track relative cam–post approach velocity and engagement timing; the rig delivered impacts with 0.1–0.6 J kinetic energy.

spans: External data included two peerreviewed simulator studies reporting PS knee wear rates under ISO conditions with sufficient metadata to reconstruct boundary conditions and surface finishes.

findings.mechanism: Articular surface wear during level walking (ISO-style input profiles)
spans: EXDWearGrow v2.0 extends the explicit dynamics kernel with a cyclebycycle update of the free surface via an Archardtype wear rule generalized for crossshear and counterface hardness, and a creep update driven by mean stress using a Findleytype law; adaptive remeshing maintains element quality as the surface evolves.
findings.span: EXDWearGrow v2.0 extends the explicit dynamics kernel with a cyclebycycle update of the free surface via an Archardtype wear rule generalized for crossshear and counterface hardness, and a creep update driven by mean stress using a Findleytype law; adaptive remeshing maintains element quality as the surface evolves.

findings.mechanism: Articular surface wear during level walking (ISO-style input profiles)
spans: The wear–creep growth loop in EXDWearGrow v2.0 was exercised on canonical problems with known solutions: for a flatonflat crawler under uniform pressure, the accumulated wear depth over 1 Mc matched the Archard solution to within 1.9%; a wedge indentation creep test reproduced the Findley prediction to within 3.5% after 10,000 s equivalent time.
